text:
A: Hi! Can you hear me okay?
B: Yes, hello. I'm Nasreen.
A: Ollie. Nice to meet you. How's your day going?
B: Okay, thank you. It's cold here, so, you know.
A: Yeah, it's freezing in London too. Our house has got this radiator that just sort of gives up after ten minutes. Where are you based?
B: Walsall.
A: Oh nice, I've not actually been. What do you do?
B: Erm, I'm between jobs at the moment. I was receptionist before, at a doctor's surgery.
A: Oh right. That sounds stressful, honestly. Everyone ringing at eight.
B: Yes. Everybody says the same thing. The last boy also said this.
A: Ha, it's the universal experience, isn't it. I'm a student, I'm at King's College in London, doing geography.
B: University. Acha. My son, he wants to go to university next year.
A: Oh, amazing. What does he want to study?
B: Erm, he says maybe computer science. Or business. He changes every week.
A: That's really normal, to be fair. I changed my mind about four times. Has he started looking at places? There's open days usually in the summer, and you can do them online now too, which helps.
B: He's looking. I don't know much about it, you know. The forms, UCAS. My daughter did it, but she did everything herself.
A: Yeah, UCAS is kind of a lot the first time. But sixth forms are normally quite good with it, they'll help him with the personal statement and stuff. And honestly, if he's thinking Birmingham, there's loads of good options up your way. Aston's really good for business.
B: Aston. Okay. I will tell him.
A: You've got a daughter as well?
B: Yes, Aleena. She's twenty-two. She lives in Birmingham now.
A: Oh nice. So she's not far.
B: No. But she's busy, you know. Young people.
A: Guilty. I should ring my mum more. So what's geography, people ask me that. I do the human side, mainly transport. Like buses, cycling, how people get around cities.
B: Buses. The bus here is always late. Wednesbury Road. Every day, twenty minutes, nothing comes, then two come together.
A: That's literally a thing! It's called bunching. One bus gets delayed, it picks up more people, gets slower, and the one behind catches up. It's kind of the classic bus problem.
B: Really? It has a name?
A: It has a name. There's papers on it. I could bore you for ages.
B: No, it's interesting. So you can fix it?
A: I wish. Not on my own. But that's the sort of job I want after uni, transport planning. Maybe TfL.
B: Then come to Walsall also, please.
A: Ha, I'll add it to the list. Do you get out much, like when it's not freezing?
B: Not so much now. Before I walked in the Arboretum. Now my knees, you know.
A: Ah, sorry. Is it a nice park?
B: Very nice. The lake, the ducks. In summer it's lovely.
A: I'll have to—
